newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS - Base metals head south for the summer.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Base metals head south for the summer.

text.p: Industrial metals were under pressure again on Tuesday as investors reduced their exposure to the sector ahead of the traditionally slow summer quarter in the Northern Hemisphere.
Not even a strike at the western world's biggest nickel producer could stem the flow of money out of the London Metal Exchange base metals' futures markets.
"The metals, in general, now look vulnerable to further spates of selling pressure...." broker Rudolf Wolff said in a daily market report.
An early rally in several metals in a knee-jerk response to news of a strike at Canadian nickel/copper producer Inco Ltd was shortlived as investors hungrily sold into the higher levels.

This soon turned prices lower, a trend which was aided by Russia's biggest nickel/copper producer, Norilsk, forecasting its 1997 output of the metals would rise by 20 percent and nine percent respectively.
"According to our plan....the Norilsk Nickel group proposes by the end of this year to hit 213,000 tonnes of nickel, 370,000 tonnes of copper...." group spokesman Sergei Vetchinin said.
The feeling among metal traders was that the Inco strike would not begin to impact on nickel prices unless it became clear that a long stoppage was in prospect.
"Nickel stocks are currently on a rising trend with Russian producers shipping to Europe and this would cushion the market from a strike, provided it was not prolonged" a trader said.

By the end of the morning copper had fallen back below $2,500 and aluminium was well below the key $1,600 a tonne level. Nickel, after rallying $300 in early trade, fell back $120 to settle at $7,180 at the end of the morning London Metal Exchange session.

Among other commodities coffee showed relative stability after recent hectic sessions with traders looking for some consolidation. At the end of the morning session on the London International Finanacial Futures Exchange July coffee futures were down around $30 a tonne.

Traders said that roasters appeared to have covered their most urgent needs and could possibly sit back for a while but they did not see prices giving up too much ground while the Brazilian crop was under threat from frost during June and July.
